answers.question: Is tap water in Qatar safe to drink?
answers.note: Kahramaa requirements and compliance only; no tap-water studies in the database
answers.answer: Tap water in Qatar is considered safe to drink according to Kahramaa's Drinking Water Quality Requirements, which ensure that the water meets health and aesthetic standards [Kahramaa_Drinking_Water_Quality_Requirements_2014.txt p.7]. answers.question: Does Qatar's tap water come from groundwater or desalination?
answers.answer: Tap water in Qatar comes primarily from desalination. Specifically, over 99.9% of Qatar’s water comes from desalinated seawater, with less than 0.01% sourced from underground aquifers [Peninsula_2025_Water_security_strategic_planning.txt p.1]. Groundwater is not the main source of tap water in Qatar.

answers.question: Can I drink the water from a well on my farm?
answers.answer: No, you cannot assume that well water is safe to drink without proper testing. Well water may contain harmful contaminants, such as bacteria, heavy metals, or chemicals, which can pose serious health risks [misconceptions.csv p.7]. To ensure safety, the water must undergo comprehensive microbiological and chemical testing according to standards like those set by KAHRAMAA and WHO [Kahramaa_Drinking_Water_Quality_Requirements_2014.txt p.7].

answers.question: Why is the water from my farm well getting saltier?
answers.answer: The water from your farm well is getting saltier because most of Qatar's groundwater is brackish, meaning it is saltier than fresh water but less salty than seawater [glossary.csv p.13]. Additionally, studies have shown that up to 95% of groundwater samples in Qatar are not suitable for agricultural irrigation, with over 60% having salinity levels that could harm crops [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. This increase in salinity is a significant challenge for farms, which often need to install desalination systems, such as reverse osmosis, to make the water usable for irrigation [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1].

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] Desalinating irrigation water
Irrigation hazard analysis - a measurement tool for the quality of water used to irrigate crops - performed on various wells located around Qatar indicated that up to 95% of samples are not suitable for agricultural irrigation, with over 60% having salinity levels which would likely cause harm to agriculture.
As such, this water is only suitable for growing very salt-tolerant crops. Thirty-four percent of the irrigation water was found to be of very high salinity hazard and medium sodium hazard, and not suitable for irrigation in almost all types of soils.
Because of this challenge of salty (“brackish”) groundwater, farms need to establish a desalination system on-site to be able to use the wells. This is typically done through a reverse osmosis, membrane-based system. Similar to the seawater desalination systems which provide the water to houses and businesses in Qatar, chemicals such as anti-scalants have to be added to the well water to help the system function correctly over time. The waste product from this process is called “brine”. The brine contains the salts and other contaminants, and chemicals, which have been removed from the well water. Brine is an environmentally challenging issue for Qatar. For seawater plants, brine is discharged off-shore, but for farms where there is no obvious disposal route, the brine is more problematic.

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] So how can groundwater in Qatar be sustainably managed? Kahramaa is actively rehabilitating and activating over 300 existing recharge wells around Qatar, to increase the direct recharge to the aquifer system in the country from the rain and subsequently improve the groundwater condition and increase its availability for water security, while at the same time extending efforts to drill and develop about 60 recharge/injection and observation wells to increase the direct recharge to storage zone and to increase the productivity of the aquifer system from the rain. Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is not easy or straightforward in Qatar due to the karstic nature of the sub-surface, but Kahramaa’s Water Projects Department budgeted 2.6 billion QAR for projects in 2019 to improve the groundwater storage zones and increase the recharge to the groundwater water aquifer system.
An even more serious issue than the decrease in quality of the groundwater is the issue of land subsidence due to the changes in the water table. For a very flat and low-lying country like Qatar, land changes can actually influence shifts along the coastline of Qatar, exacerbating any issues of sea level rise by changing the level of the land also. Research such as that ongoing at Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute ( QEERI ), part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University, a member of Qatar Foundation (QF), can help. QEERI’s Earth Science Program partnered with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the OASIS project, which intends to use satellites to help map groundwater, land subsidence and sea level changes in this region and beyond. At the same time, QEERI is developing better options for agricultural water and brine management, which can help to protect the groundwater and the environment. Research to allow more crops to be grown with less water, and better greenhouse or other cooler environment options for indoor farming can extend the growing season and reduce the burden on the groundwater system.

answers.question: Can my building's water tank contaminate the tap water?
answers.answer: The provided information does not directly address whether a building's water tank can contaminate tap water. However, it does mention that contamination can occur in the distribution system due to factors like corrosion of piping systems, microbiological activity, or ingress of windblown dust in storage tanks [Kahramaa_Drinking_Water_Quality_Requirements_2014.txt p.10]. This implies that while building water tanks themselves may not directly contaminate tap water, poor maintenance or design of such tanks could contribute to water quality issues.

answers.question: Is it allowed to use fresh groundwater to irrigate fodder?
answers.note: ANND p.20 covers the ban without approval
answers.answer: Using fresh groundwater for irrigation of fodder is restricted in Qatar. The new water law recognizes the importance of the country’s scarce high-quality fresh groundwater as an emergency source of drinking water and has instituted a ban on using it for irrigation and farming without governmental approval [ANND_Right_to_Water_in_Qatar.txt p.20]. Additionally, Qatar's National Food Security Strategy aims to reduce groundwater-based fodder production by switching to treated sewage effluent (TSE) [National_Food_Security_Strategy_2018_2023.txt p.7].

high?”42 From a rights perspective, one may argue that the cost is already too high— especially when considering how continued over-abstraction will affect future generations. However, Qatar’s agricultural sector will determine that the cost is too high only when the cost of pumping (and partially treating) groundwater exceeds the cost of desalinated seawater or TSE.43 By then, it may already be too late to save the country’s fresh groundwater resources from total destruction.

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] World Water Day: Qatar’s Groundwater Challenges
In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

answers.question: Can I water my garden with treated sewage effluent?
answers.answer: Treated sewage effluent (TSE) is wastewater that has been cleaned at treatment plants and is reused for purposes such as irrigation, landscaping, and aquifer recharge [glossary.csv p.15]. In Qatar, TSE is primarily used for green space irrigation (41.5% in 2021), followed by agricultural activity (29.7%) [PSA_Water_Statistics_2021.txt p.62]. While TSE is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. Therefore, it is possible to use TSE for watering your garden, as it is designated for landscaping and irrigation purposes.

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] World Water Day: Qatar’s Groundwater Challenges
In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

Qatar has made significant progress in recent years to rectify its water challenges. From limiting groundwater abstraction to increasing production of TSE, the situation today looks far better than it did in the early 2000s. Qatar’s successive food security strategies were designed to increase the amount of food produced in the country, which often came at the expense of the country’s agricultural sustainability. Therefore, a targeted agricultural strategy can be formulated that complements the 2024-2030 food security strategy. The objective of this agricultural strategy would be to chart a pathway for the agricultural sector to:
1) Introduce new farming technologies and methods that help farms increase production efficiency and resource utilization.
2) Reduce reliance on groundwater by aggressively ramping up the utilization of non-conventional water sources like high-quality TSE, rainwater harvesting, and atmospheric generation.
3) Achieve near universal compliance with laws regulating groundwater use through training, awareness campaigns,
and strict enforcement.

Formed in 2004, the Permanent Water Resource Committee (PWRC)8 is the highest governmental authority responsible for water resources in Qatar (Fanack Water, 2021). The Minister of State for Energy Affairs chairs the PWRC. Its responsibilities include developing and preserving water resources in the country and coordinating with relevant stakeholders to draft and propose water-related legislation to the

answers.question: How much water is stored in Qatar's strategic water reserves?
answers.answer: The strategic water reserves in Qatar are sufficient to meet demand for 5.2 days as of 2024 [Peninsula_2025_Kahramaa_water_reserves.txt p.1]. Additionally, the Water Strategic Mega Reservoirs Project, commissioned by the end of 2018, has a capacity of 1500 MIG and covers the storage requirements up to 2026 [Peninsula_2025_Kahramaa_water_reserves.txt p.1].

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] So how can groundwater in Qatar be sustainably managed? Kahramaa is actively rehabilitating and activating over 300 existing recharge wells around Qatar, to increase the direct recharge to the aquifer system in the country from the rain and subsequently improve the groundwater condition and increase its availability for water security, while at the same time extending efforts to drill and develop about 60 recharge/injection and observation wells to increase the direct recharge to storage zone and to increase the productivity of the aquifer system from the rain. Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is not easy or straightforward in Qatar due to the karstic nature of the sub-surface, but Kahramaa’s Water Projects Department budgeted 2.6 billion QAR for projects in 2019 to improve the groundwater storage zones and increase the recharge to the groundwater water aquifer system.
An even more serious issue than the decrease in quality of the groundwater is the issue of land subsidence due to the changes in the water table. For a very flat and low-lying country like Qatar, land changes can actually influence shifts along the coastline of Qatar, exacerbating any issues of sea level rise by changing the level of the land also. Research such as that ongoing at Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute ( QEERI ), part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University, a member of Qatar Foundation (QF), can help. QEERI’s Earth Science Program partnered with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the OASIS project, which intends to use satellites to help map groundwater, land subsidence and sea level changes in this region and beyond. At the same time, QEERI is developing better options for agricultural water and brine management, which can help to protect the groundwater and the environment. Research to allow more crops to be grown with less water, and better greenhouse or other cooler environment options for indoor farming can extend the growing season and reduce the burden on the groundwater system.

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] World Water Day: Qatar’s Groundwater Challenges
In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

[ANND_Right_to_Water_in_Qatar.txt p.19] Unfortunately, despite the government’s attempts to limit the use of groundwater and revitalize aquifers, the quality of groundwater continues to decline, forcing the Qatari agricultural sector to increasingly rely on brackish water desalination facilities to treat groundwater and make it suitable for agricultural use. A recent study found that just 2.7% of Qatar’s groundwater today has “excellent” suitability for drinking and 6.4% has “good” suitability (see figure 3).36 Another 15.2% has “poor” suitability and 14.6% has “very poor” suitability, while 61.1% is entirely unsuitable for human consumption.37 These figures mark a catastrophic decline compared to the 1970s (although exact data from that time period is difficult to find).
The same study found that just 6.2% of Qatar’s groundwater today has “very high suitability” for agriculture, while 24.9% has “high suitability.”38 A further 40.6% has “medium suitability” while 18.8% and 9.5% have “low” and “very low” suitability, respectively. answers.question: Do farmers pay for the groundwater they use?
answers.answer: Farmers in Qatar are allowed to withdraw groundwater free of charge, but they must comply with strict regulations. For instance, all wells must be licensed, and there are limits on the withdrawal rate and the area that can be irrigated [ANND_Right_to_Water_in_Qatar.txt p.14]. Violations of these rules can lead to severe penalties, including fines and imprisonment [ANND_Right_to_Water_in_Qatar.txt p.14].

In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

Kahramaa is actively rehabilitating and activating over 300 existing recharge wells around Qatar, to increase the direct recharge to the aquifer system in the country from the rain and subsequently improve the groundwater condition and increase its availability for water security, while at the same time extending efforts to drill and develop about 60 recharge/injection and observation wells to increase the direct recharge to storage zone and to increase the productivity of the aquifer system from the rain. Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is not easy or straightforward in Qatar due to the karstic nature of the sub-surface, but Kahramaa’s Water Projects Department budgeted 2.6 billion QAR for projects in 2019 to improve the groundwater storage zones and increase the recharge to the groundwater water aquifer system.
An even more serious issue than the decrease in quality of the groundwater is the issue of land subsidence due to the changes in the water table. For a very flat and low-lying country like Qatar, land changes can actually influence shifts along the coastline of Qatar, exacerbating any issues of sea level rise by changing the level of the land also. Research such as that ongoing at Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute ( QEERI ), part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University, a member of Qatar Foundation (QF), can help. QEERI’s Earth Science Program partnered with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the OASIS project, which intends to use satellites to help map groundwater, land subsidence and sea level changes in this region and beyond. At the same time, QEERI is developing better options for agricultural water and brine management, which can help to protect the groundwater and the environment. Research to allow more crops to be grown with less water, and better greenhouse or other cooler environment options for indoor farming can extend the growing season and reduce the burden on the groundwater system.

answers.question: How saline were Qatar's wells in 2014?
answers.answer: The salinity of Qatar's wells in 2014 was found to be very high, with over 60% of the samples having salinity levels that would likely cause harm to agriculture [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. Additionally, 34% of the irrigation water was found to be of very high salinity hazard and medium sodium hazard, making it unsuitable for irrigation in almost all types of soils [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1].

Irrigation hazard analysis - a measurement tool for the quality of water used to irrigate crops - performed on various wells located around Qatar indicated that up to 95% of samples are not suitable for agricultural irrigation, with over 60% having salinity levels which would likely cause harm to agriculture.
As such, this water is only suitable for growing very salt-tolerant crops. Thirty-four percent of the irrigation water was found to be of very high salinity hazard and medium sodium hazard, and not suitable for irrigation in almost all types of soils.
Because of this challenge of salty (“brackish”) groundwater, farms need to establish a desalination system on-site to be able to use the wells. This is typically done through a reverse osmosis, membrane-based system. Similar to the seawater desalination systems which provide the water to houses and businesses in Qatar, chemicals such as anti-scalants have to be added to the well water to help the system function correctly over time. The waste product from this process is called “brine”. The brine contains the salts and other contaminants, and chemicals, which have been removed from the well water. Brine is an environmentally challenging issue for Qatar. For seawater plants, brine is discharged off-shore, but for farms where there is no obvious disposal route, the brine is more problematic.

answers.question: Is managed aquifer recharge a feasible solution in Qatar?
answers.answer: Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is a feasible solution in Qatar, although it comes with challenges due to the karstic nature of the subsurface [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. Kahramaa, Qatar's water utility, has been actively rehabilitating and activating recharge wells to increase groundwater recharge from rainfall and improve groundwater conditions [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. Additionally, a study proposed a large-scale artificial aquifer recharge plan to increase strategic water reserves by recharging desalinated water or treated sewage effluent into the aquifers [Mohieldeen_2021_GIS_aquifer_recharge_Qatar_SciRep.txt p.1]. Experimental fieldwork has validated the feasibility of identified recharge sites, and GIS-based approaches have been used to locate optimal recharge zones [Mohieldeen_2021_GIS_aquifer_recharge_Qatar_SciRep.txt p.9]. However, MAR in Qatar is not straightforward due to the geological conditions, and efforts are ongoing to enhance groundwater storage and recharge [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1].

Kahramaa is actively rehabilitating and activating over 300 existing recharge wells around Qatar, to increase the direct recharge to the aquifer system in the country from the rain and subsequently improve the groundwater condition and increase its availability for water security, while at the same time extending efforts to drill and develop about 60 recharge/injection and observation wells to increase the direct recharge to storage zone and to increase the productivity of the aquifer system from the rain. Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is not easy or straightforward in Qatar due to the karstic nature of the sub-surface, but Kahramaa’s Water Projects Department budgeted 2.6 billion QAR for projects in 2019 to improve the groundwater storage zones and increase the recharge to the groundwater water aquifer system.
An even more serious issue than the decrease in quality of the groundwater is the issue of land subsidence due to the changes in the water table. For a very flat and low-lying country like Qatar, land changes can actually influence shifts along the coastline of Qatar, exacerbating any issues of sea level rise by changing the level of the land also. Research such as that ongoing at Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute ( QEERI ), part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University, a member of Qatar Foundation (QF), can help. QEERI’s Earth Science Program partnered with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the OASIS project, which intends to use satellites to help map groundwater, land subsidence and sea level changes in this region and beyond. At the same time, QEERI is developing better options for agricultural water and brine management, which can help to protect the groundwater and the environment. answers.question: Is land subsidence in Qatar linked to groundwater?
answers.answer: Yes, land subsidence in Qatar is linked to groundwater over-extraction. [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] World Water Day: Qatar’s Groundwater Challenges
In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] World Water Day: Qatar’s Groundwater Challenges
In line with this year’s World Water Day theme, Making the Invisible Visible, QEERI’s Senior Research Director for Water discusses Qatar’s groundwater challenges
Before the 1950s, when the first seawater desalination plant was established, groundwater was the sole provider of water for drinking and irrigation. The population of Qatar relied on wells from which freshwater was extracted, which catered to all of their water needs. Similar to other arid and desert countries, Qatar’s environment is characterized by a lack of renewable freshwater resources such as rivers and lakes. The aquifers containing Qatar’s natural fresh groundwater resources are extremely limited, and the depth to the water table varies between less than 1 meter near the coastline to more than 70 meters in some areas.
Low on groundwater resources
Since the 1970s, Qatar’s groundwater has not been replaced to the same extent to which it has been extracted. This has meant that, over time, the quality of the groundwater has been deteriorating, because as the fresh water is taken out, the seawater is pulled in from underground to fill the gap. Qatar was classified as the most water-stressed country in the world in 2019, due to a combination of low rainfall and low fresh groundwater levels, with natural renewable water resources far below the water poverty line.
Abstraction of groundwater is estimated to be approximately three to five times the rate of natural recharge. The annual total water use in agriculture rose from 140 million m3 in 1990 to 296 million m3 in 2016. However, groundwater abstraction for agricultural purposes has roughly remained unchanged at the same level since 2005 (226 – 230 million m3 /year) and additional demand has been covered by treated sewage effluent (TSE) since 2004. While treated sewage effluent is not typically used for crop irrigation, it is used to grow fodder for feeding animals.

answers.question: How does brine from farm desalination affect the land?
answers.answer: Brine from farm desalination can negatively affect the land by increasing soil salinity, which can harm agricultural productivity and degrade soil quality [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1]. This brine, a byproduct of the desalination process, contains high concentrations of salts and other contaminants, which can accumulate in the soil if not properly managed. In areas where disposal routes for brine are limited, this can lead to long-term environmental challenges, including reduced crop yields and potential harm to ecosystems [QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1].

[QEERI_2022_Qatar_Groundwater_Challenges.txt p.1] Desalinating irrigation water
Irrigation hazard analysis - a measurement tool for the quality of water used to irrigate crops - performed on various wells located around Qatar indicated that up to 95% of samples are not suitable for agricultural irrigation, with over 60% having salinity levels which would likely cause harm to agriculture.
As such, this water is only suitable for growing very salt-tolerant crops. Thirty-four percent of the irrigation water was found to be of very high salinity hazard and medium sodium hazard, and not suitable for irrigation in almost all types of soils.
Because of this challenge of salty (“brackish”) groundwater, farms need to establish a desalination system on-site to be able to use the wells. This is typically done through a reverse osmosis, membrane-based system. Similar to the seawater desalination systems which provide the water to houses and businesses in Qatar, chemicals such as anti-scalants have to be added to the well water to help the system function correctly over time. The waste product from this process is called “brine”. The brine contains the salts and other contaminants, and chemicals, which have been removed from the well water. Brine is an environmentally challenging issue for Qatar. For seawater plants, brine is discharged off-shore, but for farms where there is no obvious disposal route, the brine is more problematic.

With reverse osmosis, the product water passes through a fine membrane that the salts are unable to pass through, while the salt waste (brine) is removed and disposed. This process differs from electrodialysis, where the salts are extracted from the feedwater by using a membrane with an electrical current to separate the ions. The doctrine of riparian rights is an old one, having its origins in English common law. Specifically, persons who own land adjacent to a stream have the right to make reasonable use of the stream. Riparian users of a stream share the streamflow among themselves, and the concept of priority of use (Prior Appropriation Doctrine) is not applicable. Riparian rights cannot be sold or transferred for use on nonriparian land.
